Lead story

Ray: Okay, so here's the problem. Near a critical point, like a magnet right at the edge of losing its order, fluctuations show up at every length scale. Physicists want clean ways to pull the critical behavior out of that mess.

Ray: This paper builds on renormalization group theory, which is the toolkit for asking how a system looks as you zoom out. Using the relevant scaling operators from that theory, the authors construct complete families of fluctuation observables that are sensitive to criticality. Then they build connected correlation matrices from them. Connected just means you keep the fluctuations and subtract the averages.

Ada: Fine, but what do you do with a matrix?

Ray: You look at its eigenstates. In plain words, those are the natural patterns the matrix is made of, ranked by strength. The abstract says they reveal a hierarchy of multiscale critical correlation patterns. And the leading normalized eigenvalues, and their ratios, follow finite size scaling. That's the standard way criticality shows up as you change the system size.

Ada: And what did they test it on?

Ray: The two dimensional Ising model, the classic toy magnet. They built matrices for both the spin and the energy operators. The energy sector patterns, together with the scaling of the leading eigenvalues, provide further support for the framework.

Ada: Support, not proof. Is this a simulation or an experiment? And does it work beyond Ising, where we already know the answer?

Ray: Fair. The abstract describes a theoretical framework checked on that one model. It doesn't mention real experimental data. Extending it to systems with unknown Hamiltonians is only discussed as a possibility, so broader validation is still needed.

Ada: Does it say how many system sizes, or how precise the numbers came out?

Ray: The abstract doesn't say.

Ada: So why should anyone care?

Ray: Because if it does extend, you'd have a handle on criticality even when you don't know the underlying equations. Testing first on a model with a known answer is exactly the right first step.

Magnets and materials

Ray: On to magnets and materials. First, a fun one. When a materials search starts, you often have almost no measurements. So researchers asked a general purpose language model to write the weights of a small neural network, sixteen hidden units, straight from what it knows about materials, with no labels at all.

Ada: Wait, really? The language model just fills in the numbers? How do we know it's any good?

Ray: They ranked things and scored it with Spearman correlation. On experimental alloys, the strongest model's networks hit zero point six four to zero point seven nine. The best of five simple descriptors got zero point four seven to zero point six two. Used as the prior mean of a Gaussian process, it lifted ranking at five labels from zero point three five to zero point six nine on alloys.

Ada: And the catch?

Ray: The text we have is truncated, so the full list of target properties is unclear.

Ray: Next, angle resolved photoemission on the Kondo insulator iron antimony two. The authors see anisotropic splitting of surface states that weakens with temperature or tellurium doping, which points to magnetic order rather than a Rashba effect.

Ada: But they only say it may be consistent with surface altermagnetism.

Ray: Right. Indirect evidence, and the authors hedge themselves.

Ray: Last one. A method called PARS flags atomic environments a foundation potential handles poorly during molecular dynamics, then labels them with small first principles cells. It reports an eighty one percent lower error on titanium vacancy cluster energies. The abstract doesn't mention spin.

Ray: Metal printing. This desk is thin today, so treat these as signals. A laser powder bed fusion paper looks at heating between layers to reduce hot cracking in IN seven three eight L C, a nickel superalloy.

Ray: Exactly. And Phase3D added user profiles to its Fringe Operator software. According to the company, they bundle measurements, thresholds and alerts for consistent in process quality checks from research through production.

Weird physics corner

Ray: Okay, weird physics. Heating usually destroys order. Ice melts, magnets demagnetize. But a new theory paper shows simple quantum field theories in two space and one time dimension where order persists to arbitrarily high temperature!

Ada: Hang on. Hotter and more ordered? That's like a snowman getting sturdier in July.

Ray: Ha. Pretty much. In one model a symmetry stays broken at any temperature. In another, a Berezinskii Kosterlitz Thouless phase persists, with correlations that decay more slowly as it gets hotter. For three or more components, ordered domains actually grow with temperature.

Ada: Is this measured?

Ray: No. It's theory, using a controlled high temperature expansion, with some findings checked by functional renormalization group numerics. No experiment yet.

Ray: One more. In mixed quantum states, a symmetry can be broken strongly but preserved weakly. A monitored circuit maps exactly onto two nested percolation problems, and the paper says stabilizer simulations confirm the predictions. It even proposes an experiment without postselection.

Correlation-matrix eigenmodes give a finite-size-scaling handle on criticality

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

The abstract reports a renormalization-group framework that builds correlation matrices from spin and energy fluctuations. Its leading eigenvalues and their ratios follow finite-size scaling, and the method was tested on the 2D Ising model. Extension to unknown Hamiltonians is only discussed as a possibility, so broader validation is still needed.

THz spectroscopy of FePS3 separates ordered-phase and short-range spin effects

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

The abstract reports that frequency shifts of an interlayer shear mode appear only in the ordered phase, while linewidths track short-range spin correlations well above the Néel point. Near 3.2 T the researchers see signs of critical slowing down in a field-induced order parameter, described as consistent with that behavior. It is a clean example of an Ising-like magnet with real critical dynamics, though the slowing-down reading is suggestive rather than proven.

LLM-written network weights as a prior for few-label materials ranking

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

The abstract reports that a language model filled in the weights of a small 16-hidden-unit network without any labels, and that the network ranked experimental alloys with Spearman correlations of 0.64–0.79. The best simple descriptor scored 0.47–0.62. Used as a prior mean in a Gaussian process, it also improved ranking with just five labels. The text available is truncated, so the full set of target properties is unclear.

Inelastic neutron scattering intensity used to measure magnon quantum geometry

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

The abstract reports that the neutron-scattering cross-section in a ferromagnet encodes geometric parameters of spinor wavefunctions. That would let researchers extract the quantum geometric tensor without detailed knowledge of the spin-spin interactions. It is a tool for magnon physics rather than a discovery method, and the abstract does not name the materials measured.

ML · Magnetic Materials

ARPES hints at surface altermagnetic order in Kondo insulator FeSb2

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 6/10

The abstract reports anisotropic splitting of surface states that weakens with temperature or tellurium doping. The authors read the splitting as magnetic rather than Rashba in origin, but only say it 'may be consistent with' surface altermagnetism. The evidence is indirect, and the authors themselves hedge, which makes it an intriguing case in correlated electron materials.

Synthetic crystals from MatterGen and MLIP relaxation for diffusion pretraining

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 5/10

The abstract describes generating pretraining structures by perturbing and relaxing crystals, using MatterGen sampling and protostructure enumeration. Machine-learned interatomic potentials replace DFT for relaxation, and the approach is tested on MatBench tasks. It is a foundation-model idea aimed at small datasets, though it is not specific to magnetism.

PARS adaptively refines foundation potentials using local first-principles cells

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

During molecular dynamics, the method flags atomic environments the model handles poorly and labels them using small periodic first-principles cells. The abstract reports an 81% lower error on energies of titanium vacancy clusters. It is an active-learning recipe for adapting a general foundation potential, and the abstract does not mention spin degrees of freedom.

Parallel Monte Carlo/MD with ACE potentials scales to 670,000 atoms in LAMMPS

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 5/10

The abstract reports MPI-parallel Monte Carlo moves combined with OpenMP molecular dynamics, using ACE machine-learned potentials. It was demonstrated on Hf–Ti free energies and zirconium segregation in nanocrystalline copper. It is a practical route to Monte Carlo on realistic crystal lattices, aimed at compositional rather than magnetic order.

Additive Manufacturing

Inter-layer heating strategies for hot cracking in L-PBF IN738LC

Additive Manufacturing (journal) · 6/10

This laser powder bed fusion paper looks at whether heating between layers can reduce hot cracking in IN738LC, a nickel superalloy. No abstract was available, so the details are unconfirmed. Hot cracking is a well-known defect in printing high-strength nickel alloys, so mitigation strategies like this matter to manufacturers.

In situ alignment and continuous scanning to reduce IN718–CuCrZr interface defects

Additive Manufacturing (journal) · 5/10

Judging from the title alone, since no abstract is available, this work targets defects where two different metals meet in laser powder bed fusion. Joining dissimilar materials within one print is a hard problem, so the approach is worth watching. This reading is inferred from the title and is not a reported result.

Phase3D adds user profiles to Fringe Operator for automated decisions

TCT Magazine · 5/10

According to the company, the profiles bundle application-specific measurements, thresholds and alerts so that in-process quality checks stay consistent from R&D through production. This is a product announcement, so the claims have not been independently validated. It offers a window into how vendors package in-situ quality assurance.

Event camera used as a payload on an algal-bloom monitoring boat

arXiv · event-based vision · 3/10

The abstract describes an autonomous surface vessel carrying a water-quality sonde, side-scan sonar and an event camera. The event camera's data were collected only as context, and the machine-learning classification used the water-quality measurements rather than the event data. It is an unusual deployment of an event camera outside the lab.

Theoretical Physics

Order that persists to arbitrarily high temperature in 2+1D field theories

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

Heating usually destroys order. The abstract reports simple models combining scalars and fermions in which a symmetry stays broken at any temperature, with a BKT-type phase persisting and its correlation exponent approaching zero as temperature rises. For the n≥3 cases, the ordered domains even grow with temperature. The authors use a controlled high-temperature expansion and functional renormalization group, so this is a theory result with no experiment yet.

Critical relaxation of strong-to-weak symmetry breaking maps to nested percolation

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 6/10

In mixed quantum states, a symmetry can be broken 'strongly' yet preserved 'weakly', which requires two order parameters to describe. The abstract reports that a monitored Z2 circuit maps onto two bond-percolation problems, with autocorrelation exponents splitting into an initial-state part and an observation part. It is a neat link between quantum dynamics and classic percolation.

Hefei group proposes a unified symmetry classification for unconventional magnets

Phys.org · Quantum physics · 6/10

According to a press item, researchers at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science developed a framework for symmetry criteria and classification of unconventional magnets. That covers altermagnets and magnetic order more broadly. Only the press summary was available, so details are thin and the original paper is the place to check.

Ideal-measurement principle singles out Hilbert space and the Born rule

arXiv · quantum physics · 6/10

Imagine every observable can be measured 'ideally': repeating the measurement gives the same answer without disturbing compatible observables. The abstract states that requiring every allowed correlation in such a theory to be physically realizable selects quantum theory's Hilbert-space formalism and the Born rule. The appeal is deriving quantum structure from a physical principle rather than assuming it.

According to the headline, the technology cuts the use of heavy rare earths while keeping performance the same. Heavy rare earths such as dysprosium are a key supply pressure for EV motors. Only the headline was available, so the method and numbers are unconfirmed.

A China-Global South Project headline argues that US efforts to diversify minerals supply have yet to reduce China's leverage, ahead of talks with Xi. Only the headline was available, so specifics are unconfirmed. It is useful context on why magnet supply chains are a strategic concern.

Stockhead's headline describes a US$12bn critical minerals stockpile, and NT News covers the same story from the angle of Australian-listed firms. Both are thin on detail, so what the stockpile covers and when it starts remain unconfirmed.

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 5/10

Benchmark Mineral Intelligence looks at recent European and US rare-earth project milestones and whether they will shift supply outside China. Only the title was available, so its conclusion is unknown. It is background for the broader rare-earth magnet landscape.
